title: How to Lead Your Family Spiritually | Proverbs 22:6
metaDescription: A functional family is formed by God's Word, not the world. Explore biblical guidance for marriage and parenting from Proverbs 22:6 and more in this sermon recap.
bodyHtml:
Two men. Both spent more than forty years in ministry. Both earned doctorates. Both know the Bible inside and out. But their families tell two very different stories. One is still married to the wife of his youth after fifty-plus years, with close relationships to his children and grandchildren. The other is on his second marriage, and all three of his adult children want nothing to do with him. What made the difference? One of them actually practiced at home what he preached from the pulpit.

The state of your family shapes your future. And here is the central idea of this message in our Guidance for Today series: if your family forms your future, then your family needs to be formed by the Word of God rather than the world around you. The book of Proverbs — the Bible's how-to manual for wise living — has a surprising amount to say about how we love our spouses and raise our children. Here are four practical ways to lead your family spiritually.

1. Pursue one another (marriage)

The Bible is not shy about intimacy in marriage. Proverbs 5 puts it plainly:

"May you rejoice in the wife of your youth. A loving doe, a graceful deer — may her breasts satisfy you always, may you ever be intoxicated with her love." (Proverbs 5:18-19)

Notice it does not say the wife who is youthful, but the wife of your youth — a call to lasting, growing love. Sex is neither a god to be worshiped nor something gross to be ashamed of; it is a good gift God gives a husband and wife to bond them together for life. Like a fire in a fireplace, it warms and gives life in its right context; outside that context it can destroy. Intimacy begins naturally but it continues intentionally. If you are not intentional, couples simply drift apart over the years.

Paul makes this mutual and sacrificial:

"The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body but yields it to her husband. In the same way, the husband does not have authority over his own body but yields it to his wife." (1 Corinthians 7:3-4)

Pursuing your spouse also guards your marriage. The more satisfied and connected you are at home, the less vulnerable you are to temptation. (A clear word of grace here: if you have been betrayed, that sin belongs to the one who committed it, not to you.)

2. Change your communication (marriage)

Change your communication and you can change your relationship. Proverbs speaks directly to both spouses. To husbands:

"Her husband praises her: 'There are many virtuous and capable women in the world, but you surpass them all!'" (Proverbs 31:28-29)

You can push your wife down with constant criticism or pull her up with genuine praise. Researchers on healthy marriages have famously noted that lasting couples tend toward roughly five positive interactions for every negative one. So what is your praise-to-criticism ratio? And to wives, Proverbs is equally direct:

"Better to live in a desert than with a quarrelsome and nagging wife." (Proverbs 21:19)

The root of nagging is usually control. You are not your spouse's manager or their Holy Spirit. Speak up in love when it matters — but release the need to control and let God do the work in your spouse's heart.

3. Lead your kids to Christ (parenting)

"Train up a child in the way he should go, and even when he is old he will not depart from it." (Proverbs 22:6)

What is "the way"? Jesus said, "I am the way and the truth and the life" (John 14:6). Your number-one job as a parent is not behavior modification but spiritual transformation — leading your child to Jesus. You can raise a morally responsible child who is still spiritually bankrupt. "Train" means daily discipline, not a one-time event. Three simple practices:

  • Pray daily — short, honest prayers of blessing and thanks over your kids.
  • Attend church weekly — make Christ, and His people, a family priority.
  • Set an example — your kids learn more from who you are than what you say. The best example you can set is the gospel itself: being a person who both gives and asks for forgiveness, even from your own children.

One caution: Proverbs are wise sayings, not iron-clad promises. Children have their own free will, and we live in a broken world. But when you lay a foundation in Christ, you give your kids something to fall back on — seeds that may sprout years later.

4. Discipline your children (parenting)

"Whoever spares the rod hates their children, but the one who loves their children is careful to discipline them." (Proverbs 13:24)

Loving discipline redirects a child from foolish paths. A few guardrails: discipline must actually be done; it should flow from love rather than anger; parents should agree so children are not confused or divided; follow through decisively rather than making empty threats; and never discipline in a way that crushes the spirit. As Paul warns, "Fathers, do not embitter your children, or they will become discouraged" (Colossians 3:21). Your children should know you first as a safe, loving parent — not primarily as a disciplinarian.

The one perfect Father

Here is the honest truth: no one here is the perfect spouse or the perfect parent. If your hope is that you or your loved ones will finally get it right, that hope will fail. There is only one perfect Father, and He is God. In the story of the loving father (Luke 15), the son runs off, wastes everything, and comes home in shame — but "while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). That is the heart of God toward you.

We love because He first loved us (1 John 4:19). You cannot give a love you have not received. Before your family can be transformed, you need to be loved by the Father — and that love is offered to you in Jesus.

Takeaway

Pick just one area this week — pursue your spouse, praise instead of criticize, pray with your kids, or apologize when you're wrong. Reflection question: Have I first received the Father's love, so that I actually have love to give the people closest to me?

If you're in Livermore or anywhere across the Tri-Valley, we'd love to worship with you and walk this journey together. You were never meant to do family — or faith — alone.
